keyFindings.description: The watchdog's select can take the wrong branch, and I measured it rather than reasoning it. After `<-again` at :127 both `case <-serveStarted` and `case <-again` are ready when a second signal arrives at a broker that is already serving, and Go chooses uniformly at random, so the process calls os.Exit(1) at :140 without running the drain or srv.Shutdown and logs 'a second signal arrived while the broker was still starting up ... it has served nothing', which is false. A faithful replica of :111-141 with serveStarted closed and two SIGTERMs sent back to back took that branch in 2 of 300 runs (0.7%). The comment at :114-118 says the two readers 'cannot both fire'; the code does not give that. This is the designed use of the second signal, so the cost falls on the operator who uses the feature: in-flight requests are cut rather than finished, in the stop path this change exists to make safe. It is new in this round: round 1's code created `again` inside the drain and had no second reader. Remedy: decide on the state at the instant the second signal arrives rather than by racing two ready cases — take both signals in the watchdog and then test serveStarted with a select/default, forwarding to the drain when it is closed.

The reread listener subscribes after the first policy load, so a narrowing retag committed during a pod's boot is lost on that pod until its five-minute reload. policy.NewCurrent's first whole-namespace load runs at :264 and the LISTEN is established at :302-315; Postgres delivers nothing for a NOTIFY committed before the subscription existed, and reread.Listener.onConnected deliberately catches nothing up (reread/reread.go:142-154). So the sequence is: B reads the old tags, a peer's reread of a narrowing retag commits while B is still loading, B subscribes and binds, and B serves the old tags for up to policyRefresh. The window is the length of a namespace read — one list plus one DescribeSecret per secret, seconds for the 200-secret namespace operate.md sizes — and a rolling deploy is exactly when a pod is booting while the fleet serves, which is the deploy this issue exists for. Nothing reports it: the bind's barrier at :321-325 succeeds normally and no redial warning is logged. It is the same defect as the tester's round-1 row 8 (a draining pod missing its peers' rereads) at the other end of the lifecycle, and the comment at :282-290 reads as though the barrier closed this window too. Remedy: subscribe before the first load and refresh into the policy once it exists, or take one more load after OnConnected has fired.

Security[secret]: a kind retag's exit 0 is now one pod's answer, while the documented procedure still reads it as the fleet's. manage-a-secret.md:301-307 tells an operator to store the App key or the Google login only once the retag exits 0, and cmd/agent-secrets/secret_retag.go:174-187 (rereadRetag) enforces that by comparing the kind in the reread's answer with the kind it wrote. Both were written for a one-pod broker, where the answering pod was the fleet; the guard defends against stale store metadata, not against a stale peer. With two pods the answer is the serving pod's own policy, and a peer that did not get the notification — the fan-out failing, which main.go:427-430 answers with a WARN while the handler still returns 200 (handlers_secrets.go:126-135); a listener redialing, which catches nothing up; or the boot window in the finding above — still holds the ordinary-secret policy, and requests/machine_read.go releases a stored secret's value raw to an existing grant. So the operator writes a long-lived credential on an acknowledgement that no longer covers the fleet, and that peer releases it raw for up to five minutes. The fix need not be a durable fence: one sentence saying what exit 0 now covers — the pod that answered, with the fan-out and the five-minute reload behind it — and what to wait for before storing credential material, in the page this change already edits.

Three statements in the class the last round swept are stale again, one of them a number an operator reads. operate.md:269 says 'writing more than five secrets at once meets the broker-wide burst'; both shared bursts are ten (limits.go:189,211), and troubleshooting.md:92 already says ten. AGENTS.md:2456-2457 says the bind waits for the listener's 'first dial, successful or not'; since this round it waits on OnConnected, which pglisten runs after the LISTEN statement has succeeded (main.go:305-325, pglisten/listener.go:148-158). AGENTS.md:3023 says 'a zero drain registers neither'; the signal registration is now unconditional at main.go:111-113 and a zero drain skips only the timer and its select. Separately, limits.go:197-198 says the four fifths of the Secret Manager quota spent by every pod's reload, miss-path rereads and releases are multiplied by 'the fan-out': running N pods multiplies them, the fan-out does not — only the public reread route notifies, which handlers_secrets.go:121-125 states deliberately.

The new row measures headroom but pins no wiring: it calls oauthstore.Store.Secret directly from two goroutines and compares the elapsed time with the main-package constant, so removing the production context.WithTimeout at main.go:366-369 would not fail it. That is what the handoff says it is, and I am not asking for a row that pins the wiring; worth knowing is only that this one does not. The tester also found the figure's stated cause right but its adjective wrong — 'a few milliseconds more' for a threefold difference, which with both pooled connections open collapses to 0.7-1.6 ms on each side, so the double-digit number was connection setup and not the contention the bound exists for. The assertion is a margin, so nothing depends on either wording.
